Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish
General Hospital c. N.G.

SUPERIOR COURT

MONTREAL

THE HONOURABLE

SILVANA CONTE, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

SIR MORTIMER B. DAVIS JEWISH
GENERAL HOSPITAL

and

DR. LOUISE MINER

Plaintiffs

v.

N. G.

Defendant

and

S. G.

Interested
Person

______________________________________________________________________

TRANSCRIPTION OF A JUDGMENT

RENDERED ORALLY ON JUNE
10, 2021

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

Plaintiff is seeking a treatment order for
Defendant who is 79 years of age and has a history of psychiatric treatment
dating back 40 years, with more than 20 years at the Jewish General Hospital.

[
2
]

There have been 3 treatment orders issued since
2008, each for a duration of three years, and more than 20 hospitalizations
mostly due to non compliance with the medication.

[
3
]

The diagnosis has evolved over time but the
Court relies on the most recent medical report from Dr. Propst and Dr. Frank
dated May 31, 2021
[1]

wherein they conclude that Mr. N. G. suffers from a delusional disorder and
requires anti-psychotic medication.

[
4
]

Mr. N. G. contests the order. As a result, there
have been several postponements since September 2019 and a safeguard order in
place providing medical treatment in the interim.

[
5
]

Mr. N. G. has therefore received the treatment
required since that time and according to the testimony of Dr. Propst, he has
shown improvement and has not needed to be hospitalized since September 2019.

[
6
]

Based on the expert evidence and the evidence
provided by Mr. N. G., the Court is of the opinion that the application meets
the criteria established in
F.D
. v.
Centre universitaire de santé McGill
(Hôpital Royal-Victoria)

[2]
.

[
7
]

First, Mr. N. G. does not have the capacity to
consent to the treatment plan proposed by Plaintiff.

[
8
]

The Court retains the expert conclusion that Mr.
N. G. suffers from delusional disorder and requires anti-psychotic medication.
He has no insight into his own mental condition which Dr. Propst explains is
due to his mental illness. Mr. N. G. denies that he has any kind of mental
illness and attributes his conduct to life and circumstances. Mr. N. G. does
not recognize the benefits of the treatment plan nor the risks associated with
stopping the medication. Although, he does understand some of the side effects
from taking the medication.

[
9
]

There is also a categoric refusal to follow the
treatment plan. Mr. N. G. was clear, he does not need the medication which he
claims is redundant and he would not take it if not under a safeguard order.

[
10
]

As for the treatment plan, the Court finds that
the benefits of the plan far outweigh the disadvantages of the side effects.
Mr. N. G. has mentioned fatigue, in particular, which Dr. Propst indicated is a
common side effect. However, these side effects can be managed and the risk in
not taking the medication would result in more hospitalizations and further
isolation of Mr. N. G. who, when he is not on medication, feels harassed and
intimidated by others who misunderstand, according to Mr. N. G., his
disorganised thoughts. It will also lead to distress. Mr. N. G. cycled until
his knee injury, is active in his HLM building committee, is regularly
attending the synagogue. He is an intelligent man who can contribute to society
when he is medicated and able to organize his thoughts.

[
11
]

The 3 year order is reasonable given the long
history of mental illness and the need to ensure compliance. The injectable
medication does not require daily supervision and has been successful since
September 2019.

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

[
12
]

GRANTS
the
Plaintiffs’ application and signs the judgment hereto.
